mcqs.question: Why can't ahead-of-time (AOT) compilation reach the same peak throughput a JIT can, even though AOT has no warm-up cost?
options: AOT-compiled code is always slower than interpreted code
AOT compilers cannot perform any optimizations
JIT compiles hot methods more times than AOT does
AOT compiles before the program has ever run, so it can't use observed profile data the way a JIT can
mcqs.explanation: A JIT watches the program actually execute and optimizes for the behavior it observed (which types show up, which branches are hot); an AOT compiler has to guess statically before any run has happened. AOT code isn't slower than interpretation, AOT compilers do optimize, and recompilation count isn't the reason.

mcqs.question: A method is called exactly once from `main`, but that call contains a loop that runs a million iterations. Does HotSpot compile it?
options: No — a method called only once is never eligible for compilation
Only if it's called from more than one thread
Yes, likely — the loop's back-edge counter climbs quickly even within a single call, independent of the invocation counter
Only after the JVM restarts, since compilation happens once per process
mcqs.explanation: HotSpot tracks back-edge counts (loop iterations) separately from invocation counts, so a hot loop inside a single call can still cross the compilation threshold. Invocation count alone doesn't gate compilation, and there's no thread-count or restart requirement.

mcqs.question: What problem does tiered compilation (C1 then C2) solve that a single-tier JIT can't?
options: It avoids the fast-compile/heavy-optimization trade-off by cheaply compiling warm code first and reserving expensive optimization for methods proven genuinely hot
It eliminates the need for an interpreter entirely
It removes the possibility of deoptimization
It guarantees identical performance for every method regardless of how often it runs
mcqs.explanation: A single tier forces a choice between fast-but-weak and slow-but-strong compilation for every method; tiering applies each cost only where it's earned, using C1's collected profile data to inform C2. Tiering doesn't remove the interpreter, doesn't prevent deoptimization, and doesn't make all methods run equally fast.

mcqs.question: A call site has been polymorphic (2 types) for months and then starts seeing a dozen new types in quick succession. What happens to that call site's inline cache?
options: It stays polymorphic, since only the first two types are ever checked
It becomes megamorphic, giving up on caching and falling back to generic dispatch on every call
It reverts to monomorphic automatically, picking the most recent type
The JVM throws a compilation error and the program crashes
mcqs.explanation: Once too many distinct types show up at a call site, the inline cache exceeds what it can usefully track and gives up, falling back to a generic slower dispatch every time. It doesn't revert to monomorphic, doesn't crash the program, and doesn't disable the JIT for the whole class.

mcqs.question: A method was compiled assuming a call site is monomorphic, and a new subtype is then passed in for the first time. What does the JIT do to stay correct?
options: It ignores the new type and returns incorrect results for that call
It deoptimizes: discards the invalidated compiled code and falls back to interpretation until it can recompile with a more general assumption
It crashes the JVM with a fatal error
It silently recompiles ahead-of-time before the next full program restart
mcqs.explanation: Deoptimization exists exactly for this: when a speculative assumption breaks, the JIT safely falls back to interpreting so correctness is never compromised, and can later recompile more conservatively. It never returns wrong results, doesn't crash the JVM, and doesn't wait for a process restart.

mcqs.question: A microbenchmark calls a JVM method once, times it at 500 microseconds, and concludes the method is slow. What's wrong with the methodology?
options: The measurement is fine — a single call is the correct way to benchmark any function
500 microseconds is always too fast to be a valid JVM measurement
The benchmark captures interpreted (or low-tier) execution rather than the method's steady-state, fully-JIT-compiled performance
JVM methods cannot be benchmarked at all without disabling the garbage collector
mcqs.explanation: Without a warm-up phase, the JIT hasn't had a chance to profile and compile the method, so the number reflects interpreter overhead, not the throughput that matters in production. A single call isn't valid methodology for a JIT'd runtime, and neither the specific timing value nor GC disabling is the actual issue.
